content: Depo-Provera Overview: 1. Depo-Provera, also known as depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA), is a progestin-only hormonal contraceptive administered via injection every three months. 2. DMPA is an aqueous suspension designed for depot injection and is a derivative of the pregnane 17α-hydroxyprogesterone progestin. 3. The brand name Depo-Provera Contraceptive Injection refers to a 150 mg aqueous suspension of medroxyprogesterone acetate for intramuscular injection every 12–13 weeks, manufactured by Pfizer. 4. Another formulation, depo-subQ provera 104, is a 104 mg aqueous suspension for subcutaneous injection every 12–14 weeks, also manufactured by Pfizer. 5. Depo-subQ provera 104 was approved by the FDA in the United States for contraceptive use on December 17, 2004, and for managing endometriosis-related pain on March 25, 2005. Mechanism of Action: 1. The contraceptive effect of progestin-only methods, such as DMPA, depends on the progestin's activity and dosage. 2. High-dose progestin-only contraceptives, like injectable DMPA, primarily work by inhibiting follicular development and preventing ovulation. 3. Progestin reduces the pulse frequency of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus, leading to decreased secretion of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) by the anterior pituitary. 4. Lower FSH levels inhibit follicular development, preventing an increase in estradiol levels. 5. Progestin-induced negative feedback and the absence of estrogen-positive feedback on LH release prevent the LH surge required for ovulation. 6. The inhibition of follicular development and the absence of an LH surge effectively prevent ovulation. 7. A secondary mechanism involves altering cervical mucus, making it less penetrable to sperm. 8. DMPA use also causes the endometrium to become thin and atrophic, which theoretically could prevent implantation. However, due to its high efficacy in preventing ovulation and sperm penetration, the likelihood of fertilization is negligible. 9. There is no evidence to support prevention of implantation as a mechanism of action for DMPA. Effectiveness: 1. Clinical trials involving 8,183 women using Depo-Provera reported first-year failure rates ranging from 0% to 0.7%, with a weighted average of 0.3%. 2. For depo-subQ provera 104, trials involving 2,042 women reported a weighted average first-year failure rate of 0%. 3. A retrospective survey of 209 women using Depo-Provera reported a first-year failure rate of 2.6%. 4. Perfect use of Depo-Provera, as defined in clinical trials, results in a failure rate of 0.3%. This includes adherence to the recommended injection schedule (no more than 14–15 weeks between injections). 5. Typical use failure rates were historically the same as perfect use rates (0.3%) but were later adjusted to 3% based on retrospective survey data. Benefits: 1. Depo-Provera is highly effective in preventing pregnancy. 2. It requires administration only every 12 weeks, simplifying compliance. 3. It does not contain estrogen, avoiding risks associated with estrogen-containing contraceptives, such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), stroke, or myocardial infarction. 4. It is culturally acceptable in some settings, as injections are perceived as particularly effective and offer privacy. 5. It has minimal drug interactions compared to other hormonal contraceptives. 6. Depo-Provera reduces the risk of endometrial cancer by 80%, likely due to its anti-proliferative effects on the endometrium and suppression of ovarian follicular development. 7. It decreases the risk of iron deficiency anemia, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), ectopic pregnancy, and uterine fibroids. 8. It alleviates symptoms of endometriosis, primary dysmenorrhea, ovulation pain, and functional ovarian cysts. 9. It reduces seizure frequency in women with epilepsy and the incidence and severity of sickle cell crises in women with sickle cell disease. 10. Unlike most hormonal contraceptives, its effectiveness is not impacted by enzyme-inducing antiepileptic drugs. Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: 1. Depo-Provera can be used by breastfeeding mothers but is best delayed until six weeks postpartum to avoid heavy bleeding. 2. If not breastfeeding, it can be administered within five days postpartum. 3. Studies have shown no significant differences in birth weights or birth defects among infants exposed to DMPA through breast milk. However, a subgroup of infants whose mothers started DMPA two days postpartum had a higher incidence of doctor visits for infectious diseases in their first year. 4. Long-term studies concluded that DMPA use during pregnancy or breastfeeding does not adversely affect children's growth and development. Disadvantages and Side Effects: 1. Depo-Provera may take up to 14 days to become effective after the first injection, during which pregnancy can occur. 2. It does not protect against sexually transmitted diseases (STDs). 3. Menstrual irregularities, including amenorrhea, irregular bleeding, or spotting, are common. After one year of use, 55% of women experience amenorrhea, increasing to 68% after two years. 4. Fertility may take an average of 9–10 months to return after the last injection, with full recovery by 18 months. 5. Long-term use may lead to bone density loss, which could be irreversible in some cases. The FDA recommends limiting use to two years unless no alternative is available. Controversies and Warnings: 1. Depo-Provera has been associated with bone loss, leading to a black box warning by the FDA in 2004. The World Health Organization (WHO), however, advises against restricting its use. 2. Studies on bone density loss have shown mixed results regarding reversibility, particularly in long-term users. 3. Concerns over its use in vulnerable populations, such as women in developing countries and marginalized groups, have raised ethical questions about informed consent and coercion. 4. Depo-Provera has been used as chemical castration for male sex offenders due to its ability to suppress libido.
